name_devanagari: चन्दन्नाथ मन्दिर, बटुक् भैरब् मन्दिर || JUM0291
description_en: Temple of Baṭuk Bhairab, also known as Temple of Bhairavnāth, in the centre of Khalaṅgā (Jumla Bajār).The temple is located in the centre of a courtyard surrounded by four wings. Another courtyard, with similar dimensions, is located directly to the south. Both spaces are connected by a passage in the east. The southern courtyard contains the temple of Candannāth, also know as temple of Dattātreya (JUM0291). Access to the two courtyards is made from a single entrance, located in the southwestern part of the northern courtyard. The rooms in the wings around the temple include storerooms, a priest's room containing theakhanda bhairav dhuniand a kitchen. On the street side is a continuous row of shops rented out by the temples'ghuti, who also holds land in Bajura, Kalikot and Dolpa.The temple has a rectangular plan. The door is oriented to the south and leads to a single room. Photos of the temple's room are forbidden. The walls are built of stone and covered with plaster painted in red in the lower section and in white in the upper one. On the western facade is a niche containing a mask of Kāl Bhairava in repoussé metal. According to the inscription engraved on it, it was donated in (VS) 2062 (2005 CE). It is also forbidden to take pictures of this Bhairava mask.A hip roof of CGI sheets covers the monument.West of the temple are two large wooden poles on which are attached flags. Calledliṅga, these poles are said to measure 52 feet, in accordance with the 52 weeks in a year. They are changed each year, on the day ofghasthpana.The monument is related to the Candannāth temple, to the south. The latter is said to date from the time of the Kalyāl king Bālirāja, who is attested around 1400 CE. The current monument is of a more recent date, although no precise information is available on its antiquity.According to legend, the Nāth yogi Candannāth, cleared the land and made the Jumla region, occupied by a lake, available for agriculture. The yogi carried with him a grain of rice from Kashmir, which he planted and from there taught how to grow rice. The story takes place during the reign of the Sijapati, the lords of Sinja, who are identifiable with the Kalyāl dynasty. According to some sources, the first Kalyāl king, Bālirāja, was placed on the throne by Chandannāth himself (Shrestha 2010, p. 13), while others identify the king Medinī Varmā. The myth of the Jumla lake, which is transformed into an agricultural area by a religious figure, is not unlike that of the Kathmandu valley as described in the Buddhist text of the Svayambhūpurāṇa.
monument_assessment: Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)
references: REFERENCES Shrestha, Mandakini. 2010. “Chandan Nath Temple. A cultural heritage”, Heritage Nepal 1. 3, p. 12-17.
